text.p: Celltech Group Plc said on Tuesday it expects to enter a phase of consistent profits and neutral cash position in 1998 when two of its key drugs are scheduled to hit the markets.

Any delays in the launch of these two anti-TNF antibody drugs would fail to have dramatic consequences because of Celltech's comfortable cash position, which at the going burn rate would be depleted only after five to six years from now.
"We are talking of an enormous cushion basically," chief executive Peter Fellner told Reuters.
Celltech earlier reported a full-year pre-tax profit of 3.0 million stg after a 5.4 million stg loss the previous year.
The profit figure for the year to September 30 was inflated by an exceptional gain of 12.2 million stg on the sale of the Biologics business to Alusuisse-Lonza Group in mid-1996.
An initial payment of 31.5 million stg has been received for the acquisition of 75.1 percent of Biologics.
A further 10.5 million will be paid by the end of 1997 to be followed by another eight million the year after.
Celltech's underlying burn rate is currently six million stg and this may increase to eight million next year.
"Even if that increases to about eight next year, you can see that we essentially have almost an indefinite amount of cash now," said Fellner.

"Unless some unusual or interesting opportunity appears we don not for our normal operations have to go back to our shareholders," he added. Celltech expects the two drugs it has jointly developed with Bayer to hit the markets in 1998 as a crucial phase III study into one of them, BAYX-1351, is nearing completion. If succesfull, Bayer will speed up the process of making the other anti-TNF antibody drug, BAY10-3356, ripe for launch.
"If our products are sucessfully launched in 1998...we will actually go into profit and our own planning suggests we will actually remain in profit from that time," Fellner said.
If all goes according to plans, Celltech will expand its research and development programme, moving deeper into areas such as immunity and gene therapy.
R&D investment in the 1996/97 financial year is expectd to rise by about 20 percent after it rose to 17.4 million stg from 71.1 million in the year to September 30.
Fellner said Celltech will continue to develop drugs with major pharmaceutical firms.

But Celltech now has enough expertise that it no longer needs a European partner at the early stages of development of some drugs, such as CDP 850, which is a novel treatment for psoriasis, Fellner said.
